#584. Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water

Earth may have created a substantial amount of its own water as the planet was forming, rather than relying entirely on comets, meteorites, or other objects to deliver it from space. New research published in Nature Geoscience suggests that chemical reactions between rocky pebbles and the hydrogen-rich atmosphere of the young Earth could have produced enormous quantities of water.

The discovery offers a new explanation for how our planet acquired one of the most important ingredients for life. It also raises the possibility that other rocky planets throughout the universe could generate water through similar processes, potentially making habitable worlds more common than previously thought.

Researchers at The University of New Mexico investigated this possibility by recreating some of the extreme conditions that existed during Earth's formation. The study was led by graduate student Susmita Garai, along with Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Peter Olson. Their experiments examined what happens when rocks containing iron react with hydrogen at extremely high temperatures.

"Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism," explained Sharp. "In order to evaluate the possibility of 'pebble' rain' being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high-temperature experiments. Dr. Garai's efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high temperature environment of the Early Earth's atmosphere."

A New Explanation for the Origin of Earth's Water

For decades, scientists have debated where Earth's water originally came from. One prominent theory suggests that much of it was transported to the developing planet by icy material originating in the colder, more distant regions of the early solar system.

According to this explanation, water-rich objects, including small icy pebbles, traveled inward and eventually contributed to Earth's water supply. However, researchers have struggled to fully explain how enough of this material could have reached our planet from such great distances. There are also unresolved questions about whether this delivery process accounts for Earth's chemical composition.

The new study investigates a different route by which water could have appeared. Instead of arriving already contained in ice or other materials, water may have been produced directly through reactions involving the rocky ingredients that built Earth and the gases surrounding it.

During the planet's earliest stages, countless small pieces of rock gradually came together to form a larger body. Scientists refer to this growth process as pebble accretion. As Earth gained mass, it could have accumulated a dense atmosphere containing large amounts of hydrogen, with temperatures and pressures far higher than those found on the planet today.

Under those conditions, rocky pebbles falling through the atmosphere could have triggered a remarkable chemical reaction. Hydrogen in the surrounding gas would react with iron oxide inside the silicate rocks, transforming the iron oxide into metallic iron while releasing water vapor.

Experiments Reveal Water Can Form in Minutes

To determine whether this process could actually occur, the researchers exposed samples of silicate rock to temperatures ranging from 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius. They conducted experiments using flowing hydrogen gas and repeated the tests with helium to provide a comparison. Each experiment ran for between 15 minutes and three hours.

The results provided strong evidence that the proposed reaction works under these extreme conditions. When the rocks were heated in hydrogen, almost 80% of their iron oxide was transformed into metallic iron, with water vapor produced during the reaction.

In contrast, the researchers did not observe the same reaction when helium was used instead of hydrogen. This difference confirmed that hydrogen played a crucial role in generating the water.

The speed and scale of the reaction were especially striking. Although the scientists had expected some water to form, the results suggested that the process could have been far more productive than anticipated. When they extended their experimental findings to conditions on the early Earth, their calculations indicated that the mechanism might have generated hundreds of oceans' worth of water.

"We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans' worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 ½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have," said Sharp.

Earth's Fiery Beginnings May Have Helped Create Its Oceans

These findings suggest that the conditions of Earth's formation may have actively contributed to its water supply. Rather than being entirely dependent on water delivered from elsewhere in the solar system, the growing planet may have possessed the ingredients needed to manufacture water through its own chemical reactions.

The implications extend well beyond Earth. If rocky planets around other stars develop similarly hot, hydrogen-rich atmospheres during their formation, they might also produce substantial amounts of water as rocky material accumulates.

This possibility could have important consequences for understanding how common water is across the universe. A process that naturally occurs during the formation of Earth-sized planets would mean that obtaining water might not require the right icy objects to arrive from distant regions of a planetary system.

Could Other Earth-Like Planets Make Their Own Water?

The research also adds to growing interest in pebble accretion as an explanation for how planets form. Although the concept has gained attention relatively recently, it has already helped scientists address several longstanding questions about planetary development.

"The idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. It's only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation," Sharp said. "And now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life."

There are still important uncertainties to resolve. While the experiments show that rocky material can generate water when exposed to hydrogen under conditions resembling those of the early Earth, they do not establish how much of our planet's present water supply was actually produced this way. Additional research will be needed to determine the contribution of this mechanism compared with water delivered by comets, meteorites, and other sources.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important process that may have shaped Earth billions of years ago. They also suggest that the ability to produce water could be built into the formation of rocky planets themselves, opening new possibilities for understanding where water, and perhaps life, might exist beyond our solar system.

Materials provided by University of New Mexico. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#583. Best OLED TVs of 2026: LG, Samsung, Sony, and More

The TV landscape has changed dramatically this past year. New art televisions now look like matte-finish paintings on the wall. RGB televisions use red, green, and blue lights for accurate color. But OLED televisions still reign supreme for deep and rich blacks. They can control individual pixels or turn them off completely for an inky, cinematic look.

Fortunately, probably because of this intense competition, many OLED televisions are more affordable than ever. After testing many of the best models this year, I narrowed down my favorites to the ones that truly deserve a place on your TV stand.

For more home theater and audio recommendations, check out related guides to the Best RGB TVs, Best Home Theater Projectors, and Best Soundbars. Or, if you don't know where to start, read our guide on How to Buy the Right TV in 2026.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

An OLED television is different from LCD displays like LED and micro-RGB TVs. OLED (organic light-emitting diode) uses special organic material that lights up when fed electricity. That means each individual pixel can be turned completely on and off independently.

For movies and shows, that means dark scenes look more realistic and show extra shadow detail. In practice, when Star-Lord flops onto the screen in the intro of Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2, you can see more details in his dark gray suit—folds, ripples, and belts.

A good rule of thumb? Choose your OLED size based on the size of the room and how far away you will sit from the screen.

Larger sizes are more expensive—doubly so for OLED models. While an 85-inch OLED screen will look spectacular, it will cost you, and will be really hard to move around and install.

For most larger living rooms or group viewing areas, 65 inches is the standard. Anytime we quote a price or link to a retailer below, assume we are linking to the 65-inch version of the TV (unless we specifically call out another size).

I've tested a lot of RGB TVs in 2026, and put them through the wringer against OLED models, often in the same room. In my results, OLED TVs still generally have the upper hand because individual pixels can be dimmed dark gray or turned off completely. Dark scenes in movies like The Batman look more realistic on an OLED than an RGB TV. However, I expect RGB TV tech to improve quickly. By next year, it might finally trump OLED.

What sets the Samsung S95H apart from other OLED models is a brighter, clearer, and more colorful picture. It's simply the best OLED display I’ve tested this year.

Picture quality is outstanding. Extra features like the AI picture optimizer actually make a big difference in eking out even more detail. For example, Game of Thrones looked a bit dark at first watch—that is, until the AI optimizer kicked in and made everything more visible, no diving into settings necessary.

The S95H also has a new, sleek design this year. The main display sits just in front of a silver bezel, giving it a more modern, picture-frame look. (The previous Samsung S95F was all black with no silver bezel.) Another win for the S95H is that it no longer requires the Samsung One Connect breakout box to use. You can use one if you want (purchased separately), but the HDMI ports are now on the TV itself, which I find far more convenient for keeping my gear in one place near my TV. The remote is still logical and intuitive, though I can't say the same for the Tizen operating system (you get used to it).

Using the word “budget” to describe any OLED television might seem misplaced. However, the LG B6 bucks the trend at $1,300, and performed commendably in most of my tests.

I love how easy it is to set up using the LG ThinQ app, which does most of the heavy lifting, like choosing which apps to install by default. The all-black, unassuming design (no silver accents here), won't turn heads, but at this price, that's expected.

Picture quality is great for the price, but obviously outclassed by pricier models like the midrange LG C6 and flagship LG G6. Still, some of my test movies, like The Creator, looked surprisingly cinematic and colorful for a budget TV. For more challenging scenes (dark scenes in Game of Thrones and The Batman), be ready to tweak the settings dial in the picture. The 120-Hz refresh rate makes this TV no slouch for gaming, either—Resident Evil: Requiem running on a high-end gaming PC looks photorealistic.

A Sony OLED only makes sense for gaming, especially on a Sony Playstation 5. The Sony Bravia 8 II runs at a common 120-Hz refresh rate, but works seamlessly with the PS5 in ways other TVs don't. It can automatically enable features like HDR tone mapping (for a more colorful picture) and low-latency gaming mode (for a slight advantage in quick controller nudges).

Of course, the Bravia 8 II is excellent outside of gaming too. For movie night, we found that 4K and even older 1080p HD movies and shows looked crisp and colorful, with deep blacks. Off-angle viewing is also exceptional, helping those sitting off to the side in your entertainment room to still enjoy the experience without any weird dimming or glare. It also runs Google TV OS, one of the easiest operating systems to use. Google Gemini in particular is great at searching for content—prompts like “Show me the best psychological thrillers from the '90s” actually worked.

One downside is ports—this TV only has two HDMI 2.1 ports. Most premium models these days have four. Viewing in especially bright rooms can be challenging, but that is a common problem with many OLED TVs.

Yes, this model was replaced by the LG G6 (which we are still testing), but honestly, the 2025 LG G5 is a crown jewel of OLED televisions, and on sale for much less than the G6. With deep and rich blacks, a speedy operating system, and exceptional gaming features like a 165-Hz refresh rate, it’s one of my favorite premium OLED TVs.

I tested the movie Tron: Ares on this television and was blown away by the picture quality. The OLED tech made the blacks look so rich and inky, even the helmet on the main character looked realistic, with clearly visible crevices and shadows on his uniform.

Sound is also premium—the G5 supports Dolby Atmos surround sound on the television itself, making movies sound more like they do in the theater straight out of the box (though I would still recommend a soundbar).

Sure, the Samsung S95H is the better overall pick, but the G5 surprised and delighted me with things like its lightning-fast processor, operating system, and size options (it goes all the way up to a 97-inch model that costs $25,000).

Roku Pro Series OLED for $1,200: If you're OLED-curious, on a budget, and a big fan of the Roku operating system, consider the Roku Pro Series OLED. It's incredibly easy to set up, runs on Roku's simple operating system, and has a great remote-finding button on the side of the TV itself. It's even cheaper than the LG B6, though it isn't as bright or as colorful.

Sony Bravia 6 OLED for $2,000: This entry-level OLED launched in 2025 and has been on sale at up to 40 percent off, putting it on the same price tier as the LG B6. One reason to pick the Bravia 6 over the LG B6 is operating system—the Bravia 6 runs on Google TV, which I strongly prefer for quick voice searches using Google Gemini compared to webOS on the LG models. The B6 has a superior picture and deeper blacks, though.

For picture quality, OLED TVs still reign supreme because they can control individual pixels and turn them off completely. However, over the last year, art TVs and RGB TVs have started to take more and more real estate on store shelves. Some brands, like Hisense and TCL, have a totally OLED-free TV lineup for 2026, switching focus to RGB and mini-LED. If you're curious about the competition, I’ve listed a few other TV types to consider.

An art TV: Samsung The Frame Pro (2026)I absolutely loved this premium art television. I mounted it on the wall in my office for a couple of months, showcasing shipwrecks and masterpiece paintings daily. The matte finish and anti-glare tech make this television able to display more like a piece of wall art in a museum than a shiny, reflective black box. The Pro version in particular offers far better picture quality for TV shows and movies than other art TVs on the market.

An RGB TV: LG Micro RGB Evo 75-inchMy top pick for an RGB television, the LG Micro RGB Evo is highly customizable in terms of picture quality. You can tweak just about every color and brightness setting to make sure dark scenes look textured and clear and colors look realistic, not oversaturated. It's unfortunately only available in larger sizes: 75, 86, and 100-inches.

A projector: AWOL Vision Aetherion MaxIf you want to skip the rectangular box and TV stand altogether, consider a high-end, ultra-short-throw projector like the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max. While I do recommend using a projector screen, I’ve found some high-end projectors like this one can even outclass OLED in terms of color richness and black depth.

The WIRED reviews team is busy testing the ever-popular midrange LG C6 and premium LG G6. Given their past history, we expect them to be strong contenders for top accolades.

#582. Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. Fans with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, recall Rummenigge as one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or — in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer, in 1996.

That long drought ended on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, picking up the 2026 trophy at a ceremony held, as a one-off, in his native London.

"I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special,” he said on stage.

Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane later told British sports streaming plaftorm DAZN.

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16, finished third. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain as well as the La Liga title. Kylian Mbappe came in second.

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season made for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 159 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," Vincent Kompany said of Kane last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now — it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

Kane continues to improve at 33, a point when many footballers start to regress. Though he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions League against Arsenal last week. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all-round game. "The pass was one of my best ones," Kane said after the match. "I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals."

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach, Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after Kane joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care — he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone, and that is his mindset, and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills, Tuchel said in September as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic. "He is a complete package."

There are detractors who point to perceived "stat-padding," or scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams and a lot less money, than in England. Though Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

Kane winning the award is also a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga.

Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain perhaps makes Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward, something he admitted in his speech. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.

"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs, I had a lot of loan moves, I had to fight my way to be the very best right now, and I hope that can give you determination as well," Kane said in his speech.

For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023, before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential," Defoe said. "He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean. … With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggests that he could get better still.

This article was first published on October 22, 2026. It was updated on October 27 after Harry Kane won the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

#580. Cosm rides premium moviegoing wave with more immersive screenings and a wider library

The next big thing in premium large format theatrical viewing takes inspiration from the stars.

Cosm, an immersive entertainment technology company, got its start programming planetariums — its name a combination of "cosmos" and "colosseum." The company's massive, domed screens first offered guests a view of the universe, now they mimic courtside seats at sports venues around the world and drop film fans into some of Hollywood's most iconic sets.

At a time when the theatrical industry is seeing its biggest growth from the sale of premium large format, or PLF, tickets, Cosm seeks to offer a fresh take on an elevated viewing experience. And it's quickly expanding both its footprint and its content library.

Since 2024, Cosm has opened four theaters — near Los Angeles, Dallas, Atlanta and Detroit — with a Cleveland hub set to open in 2027. These experimental venues have garnered the attention of sports fans, screening live matchups in an arena-like environment. Showings often sell out, according to Cosm.

More recently, Cosm has partnered with Hollywood studios like Warner Bros., now a part of Skydance, to bring the likes of "The Matrix," "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" and "It" to its locations. Cosm recently signed a deal with Universal, which will bring "Shrek" to its domes in December.

The agreements mark a lucrative new chapter for the privately held Cosm, expanding its audience reach and viewing opportunities beyond timed, live events.

As a privately held company, Cosm doesn't disclose its financials. Tickets cost anywhere from $18 for a matinee to around $70 for prime seats or in-demand showings. That doesn't include added fees for concessions or items from special, themed menus tied to screenings.

Sony invested $100 million in the company in June, taking a minority stake and placing Sony Pictures Entertainment Chairman and CEO Ravi Ahuja onto its board of directors.

Cosm also counts among its investors Cosm chairman Steve Winn's firm, Mirasol Capital; former Milwaukee Bucks co-owner Marc Lasry's Avenue Sports Fund; Rocket Mortgage co-founder Dan Gilbert's Rock; and David Blitzer, managing partner of the New Jersey Devils and Philadelphia 76ers, who invested through his firm Bolt Ventures.

"Cosm is really early in its growth trajectory at the moment, and we saw an opportunity to partner with the company at, what I would say is at, a very important stage in its development," Jay Levine, chief strategy and business operations officer at Sony, told CNBC. "They have about five locations with the goal of a pretty significant rollout. And the real reason why we did it was it gave us a lot of exposure to a growing distribution and what we deem an experiential platform that we think has long-term potential."

Sony has made several plays in the theatrical space in recent years. It bought Alamo Drafthouse in 2024 and entered a long-term lease to reopen and restore the iconic Cinerama Dome in Los Angeles in July of this year.

"Our experiences strategy is around tech, it's around fandom, and it's around new and innovative approaches to content distribution," Levine said. "For us, we're all about these differentiated experiences."

Cosm's 87-foot-diameter, concave screens drop viewers into the middle of the action, whether it's an NFL game or inside the world of "The Matrix." The company's forthcoming Cleveland location will have an even bigger dome, at 100 feet in diameter.

The experience is akin to that of the Sphere in Las Vegas, which has garnered headlines since opening in 2023 for hosting high-profile concerts and events.

"People absolutely love to live out what they love in fandom, just like wearing a sports jersey," Alexis Scalice, head of Cosm Studios, told CNBC. "And I love that I'm seeing that same behavior happen with cinema."

Stadium-style seating is nestled within each Cosm dome, with booths and tables set on each level. The dome's width is such that it fills much of the viewer's periphery, giving the sensation that they are part of the on-screen environment.

The Los Angeles and Dallas locations have capacity for around 350 seats each, while the newer domes in Atlanta and Detroit have up to 500 available seats. Cosm has not shared how many seats the Cleveland location will have, but with its larger screen it is expected to have a larger number of seats.

For live sports events, Cosm has specialty cameras mounted in arenas that broadcast back to the dome, creating the illusion of being on the field of play.

For theatrical features, the film is played in a large rectangle in the center of the dome and the background is transformed to extend the scene.

In Cosm's presentation of "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," for example, during the iconic scene where thousands of Hogwarts acceptance letters flood through the fireplace and into a living room, the background is swarmed with animated envelopes.

Cosm has partnered with experiential production company Little Cinema and creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and environments for each scene of a film released in the dome. From storyboarding to post-production, this process can take up to a year as Cosm, the participating studio and the visual effects artists craft and render each moment.

"We really work hard not to take away from the story, so the film remains the hero in the narrative," Scalice said. "Working very closely with Warner Bros. and our creative partners to make sure that we're not detracting too much from the story, but we're enhancing those moments for more elevated emotional response."

With the exception of "It," which was released in 2017, Cosm's theatrical offerings thus far have been films that were released decades ago and that typically have long-established fan bases.

That helps Cosm leverage what Scalice called "that nostalgia factor" — "parents coming in that ... grew up on this, and they want to share it with their children."

"We can reinvigorate these legendary films," she added.

Cosm has dabbled across genres — horror, fantasy, science fiction — and also demographics — family-friendly and R-rated. "Shrek," set to debut Dec. 16, will be its first foray into animation.

"The thing that's so incredible about it is everybody thought initially it's just going to be working for sports, and when you look at what they've done, a lot of the titles with 'Harry Potter,' with 'Shrek,' and some of the other ones, I mean, the fill rates are actually incredible," Sony's Levine said.

Studios and theatrical exhibitors alike are looking for innovative ways to showcase Hollywood's product to moviegoers, especially as major shifts in viewing habits have disrupted the business.

In the post-pandemic era, the cinema space has been defined by fewer screens and fewer moviegoers, but those declines have been masked by higher movie ticket prices, particularly for PLF experiences.

These elevated offerings — think Imax, Dolby Cinema, ScreenX and 4DX — have bigger screens and better sound or introduce a unique experience, such as moving seats and fog machines. They're particularly popular with Gen Z and millennials, who've yet to be deterred by rising average ticket prices.

While an average standard movie ticket costs around $13, premium tickets average more than $18 each, according to data from EntTelligence.

Prices for Cosm's events fluctuate based on showtime and venue. Sony's Levine said the company's ticket prices and attendance rates are "higher than I think anybody really would have thought."

Unlike Cosm's sports offerings, which can also be viewed from outside the dome from its hall and deck viewing areas at a lower price, theatrical presentations are only available in the dome.

"They have no problem selling these tickets because people want to experience these things, like an immersive format," said Mike Polydoros, CEO at cinema marketing firm PaperAirplane Media. "That is something they can't get at home."

#579. Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery

Deep inside South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, scientists have uncovered a surprising clue about an extinct human relative that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. For the first time, researchers have recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils, revealing evidence that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.

The discovery, published in the journal Cell, raises an extraordinary possibility. The cave could represent the earliest known burial location reserved for one sex by a human relative other than Homo sapiens.

Homo naledi lived approximately 335,000 to 241,000 years ago and has fascinated scientists since its discovery in 2013. This extinct species combined primitive features resembling those of apes with other characteristics more closely associated with modern humans.

A Strange Mystery Hidden in Ancient Human Fossils

One of the biggest puzzles surrounding Homo naledi involves the remarkably similar appearance of adult fossils recovered from the cave's Dinaledi Chamber. For more than a decade, researchers have struggled to explain why these individuals showed so little of the physical variation normally associated with differences between males and females.

To investigate, an international research team involving the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other institutions turned to proteins preserved in the ancient remains.

The scientists used a technique involving gentle acid etching to recover tiny protein fragments known as peptides from fossilized tooth enamel. This approach allowed them to collect samples while minimizing damage to the valuable fossils. In total, they examined 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 different individuals.

The researchers specifically searched for Amelogenin-Y, a protein produced from a gene on the male Y chromosome. Surprisingly, they found no evidence of this male-specific marker.

To verify that their findings were reliable, specialists at the University of York's chemistry facility examined the amino acids in the samples. Their analysis confirmed that the proteins were genuinely ancient rather than the result of contamination from modern sources.

Could Homo naledi Have Had an All-Female Burial Site?

Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York's Department of Chemistry, said: "The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.

"These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins."

The results raise important questions about how Homo naledi individuals lived, organized their communities, and treated their dead. If the Dinaledi Chamber was intentionally used only for females, it could point to surprisingly elaborate social customs among these ancient human relatives.

Such a practice might even suggest symbolic burial traditions once believed to be exclusive to Homo sapiens, or modern humans.

However, the researchers emphasize that an all-female burial site is not the only possible interpretation of the evidence.

Another explanation involves the genetics of Homo naledi itself. If the population lived in extreme isolation, the gene responsible for producing Amelogenin-Y could have undergone a mutation or disappeared entirely.

Under that scenario, some of the individuals could actually have been male, even though their teeth did not contain the protein normally used to identify them.

Ancient Tooth Enamel Opens a New Window Into Human Evolution

The ability to recover proteins from fossils this old is particularly valuable because tooth enamel can protect biological material for extraordinarily long periods.

Palesa Madupe, who carried out the research during her postdoctoral work at the University of Copenhagen, explained why teeth offer such an important source of evidence.

"Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel -- the hardest tissue in the human body -- shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.

"This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it's probably because they could have all belonged to one sex."

The research represents the largest collection of individuals from an extinct hominin species ever examined using ancient protein analysis.

Whether the fossils belong entirely to females or include males with an unusual genetic signature, the discovery provides an important new perspective on Homo naledi. It also demonstrates how proteins preserved in ancient teeth can reveal clues about extinct human relatives that their bones alone cannot provide.

As researchers continue investigating the mystery, the findings could reshape our understanding of the social lives and possible burial traditions of ancient human species.

#578. Africa's first Youth Olympics open in Senegal amid hope and scrutiny

Senegal is hosting Africa's first Youth Olympics, with 2,700 young athletes competing in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. The Games bring pride and hope, but also questions over cost, rights and legacy.

On the final day of October, what may well be the final Summer Youth Olympics ever will begin. It will be the first on African soil as around 2,700 athletes aged 15-17 arrive in Senegal to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports.

Hosted in eight venues across three locations – Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the capital – these Games are seen by many as a prelude to Africa hosting a full Olympics one day in the future.

"I'm really excited about the Youth Olympic Games because, for the first time, I'll be representing our country," 15-year-old judoka Aisha Diop who is competing for Senegal told DW.

"I am very proud to be able to represent my country at these Games. This will really motivate young African athletes because they will improve, and they will want to continue playing sports now that the Youth Games have been held here."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 Youth Games in Senegal will also be a first beyond the history it is making in Africa.

"Of the 2,700 athletes who will be competing in Dakar, there will be a 50-50 split between men and women," Olivia Nloga, Chief Brand Promotion Officer on the organizing committee, told DW.

"But this parity isn't just reflected in the overall figure. This gender parity will also be reflected in each event and in each sport where such parity actually exists."

Several sports are also making their debut at the Youth Olympic Games, such as five-a-side baseball, kung fu and the Senegalese specialty of beach wrestling. There's also a refugee team at the Youth Olympic Games for the first time.

"As I said earlier, the Youth Olympic Games aren't just about sports, and they aren't just about infrastructure," said Nloga.

"For us, it was also important to use this time to build on and reinforce the idea that these Games in Senegal are a celebration for the people. We did this by investing in culture—for example, through a fashion show and a program called Yi-sol, which is a mural project on the city's walls."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other projects designed to celebrate the people include music, and a local student designed the mascot. The biggest focus of all though, is on creating sustainability for the young people of Senegal.

"We did so through a program that is very important to us – one that is close to our hearts, namely, the Olympic Civic and Sports Certificate," Nloga said.

"We traveled to schools throughout Senegal and worked with more than 1,000 instructors to reach and make an impact on more than one million young Senegalese children who, during this hiatus, were exposed to and educated about the values of the Olympic Movement."

With recent flooding in the country, there were concerns that infrastructure would have been affected, but Nloga insisted that flood risk had long been in the planning.

"The prime minister held an interdepartmental meeting during which he established a task force to ensure that the necessary arrangements and follow-up measures are put in place to safeguard both the competition venues and the accommodation sites."

With Formula 1 confirming its return to Africa earlier in October, global sport is slowly becoming a more regular event in Africa. As a result though, there have been questions asked about the legacy of such events.

Many in Senegal concerned by the high cost of living and unemployment will see these Games as an unnecessary expense. For the Senegalese authorities though, they are an opportunity for long-term investment in the country's young people as well as infrastructure. There is also the hope that this will make Dakar a major tourist destination.

There was further criticism of the Games being in Senegal from Human Rights Watch (HRW), with the NGO calling on the Senegalese authorities to change their stance on the LGBTQ+ community.

"You are welcoming all of the world. It shouldn't be 'you are welcome to our country, except this, except that,'" Larissa Kojoue from HRW told DW.

"Anti-LGBT legislation and that crackdown that is going on, they contradict the Olympic movement, the Olympic Charter, and also various human rights convention that the country has signed."

Earlier this year, Senegal President Bassirou Diomaye Faye signed into law new legislation on same-sex relations that have proved contentious abroad despite broad political support within the majority Muslim country's parliament. Several human rights groups had voiced concerns about the bill, including warning that it would dissuade people at risk of illnesses like HIV/AIDS from seeking help.

The Games were set to see the return of Russians to Olympic competition under their own colours after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) lifted their suspension in July.

However, the Russian Athletics Federation (RusAF) released a statement the day before the opening ceremony saying the reported 13 athletes (and 10 coaches) had been exluded from the competition. They demanded an explanation and asked for the decision to be reconsidered.

"The IOC-endorsed position was clear in its direction: young athletes holding Russian or Belarusian passports should no longer be restricted from international youth competitions. That principle should apply to Dakar 2026," read the statement.

Despite the IOC's ruling, each federation can still decide whether to authorize Russian participation. World Athletics, has clearly upheld their ban, while swimming and judo have allowed Russian athletes back.

"This has enabled World Athletics to pursue its own exclusory agenda in the face of clear and just directions from the IOC. This activism is only detrimental to youth sports, with the result being that Russian young athletes will be denied the opportunity to compete at these Games."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite the various concerns, there is an overriding hope that the Games will be prove beneficial for all involved.

"What makes the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar special is that they are also rooted in Senegal's extremely strong sporting culture," Nloga said.

"Every evening, when you take a stroll along the Corniche in Dakar, you're struck by the number of people you see exercising, regardless of their age or physical condition. What we'll be offering during these Olympic Games is also an immersion into Senegalese life – into the way sports are just as much a part of Senegalese identity."

This article was updated on October 30, 2026 to reflect the change in situation for Russian athletes at the Games.

#576. Exclusive: Your Smartphone Camera Could Get a Big Upgrade With This Tech

One of the most essential pieces of technology that makes your phone’s camera work was created in 1974, and it hasn’t changed much since.

When you snap a photo with your smartphone, the camera captures light and converts it into electrical signals to build a digital image. But the Bayer filter—a red, green, and blue layer that sits above the sensor and adds color to your images—absorbs and wastes around 60 percent of that light before it can reach the sensor. To make a red pixel, the filter blocks and throws away blue and green light.

Now, the Boston company Metalenz has acquired an Israeli startup called PxE Holographic Imaging, which has developed a new optical layer called a HoloCoder. This microscopic structure sits directly on top of the image sensor and diffracts light, bending the light waves rather than absorbing them.

With the HoloCoder redirecting the light waves toward the sensor’s pixels instead of blocking them, the camera sensor can collect up to a claimed 2.5 times more light. Such a leap in light-gathering ability could dramatically improve a smartphone's low-light photography and dynamic range.

There's a surprising secondary benefit too: HoloCoder technology can capture 3D depth information at the same time. Most smartphones use secondary cameras, dedicated depth sensors, or AI guesswork to figure out the distance between the camera and the subject in order to judge how much depth should be shown in features like portrait mode. By merging light sensing and depth sensing into one layer, the HoloCoder promises to simplify the electronics on the back of your smartphone, saving space and processing power.

Some layers are no longer required on a camera system using PxE’s HoloCoder technology.

The acquisition of PxE—details of which were not disclosed—makes sense for Metalenz. The company launched publicly in 2021 and pioneered the commercialization of metasurfaces, a flat-lens system with nanostructures that bend light, reducing the need for multiple lens elements over the camera sensor while also capturing more light. The company has shipped more than 300 million of these metasurface optics to consumer devices today.

The technology can also capture polarization data, and Metalenz is working with Qualcomm to create a more effective, secure facial biometric authentication system for Android called Polar ID to rival Apple's Face ID, expected to arrive on consumer devices at the end of 2027.

Rob Devlin, Metalenz CEO and cofounder, tells WIRED that PxE's approach mirrors his own company's by patterning microscopic structures directly onto an image sensor to unlock light data that conventional camera systems throw away.

A New Lens Technology Is Primed to Jump-Start Phone Cameras

Smartphone Cameras Might Soon Capture Polarization Data

Polar ID Is the Face ID Rival for Android Phones, and Could Even Beat Apple

This Company Has Figured Out a Way to Make Face ID Invisible

“Apple, Samsung, Google—everyone is fighting to improve the visible camera every year, right?" Devlin says. "A lot of what they're doing is investing hundreds of millions of dollars into software to try to somehow improve it, but the downside of that is that once information is lost when you're absorbing all of that light, you can't really buy it back, even if you're throwing all of the software into the world at it.”

Low-light photography and night-time video capture could see dramatic improvements with the HoloCoder system. In high-contrast scenes—like taking a selfie in front of a bright window—the sensor can capture more light and better re-create the scene without blowing out highlights or drowning shadows in noise.

PxE's technology isn't on the market yet, but as Metalenz has already developed a supply chain, processed an image pipeline, and set up machine learning algorithms on how to take advantage of these new data streams, Devlin thinks PxE's HoloCoder will be able to fit neatly into its platform and “completely disrupt" the visible sensing market. While the HoloCoder functions as a diffractive optic rather than a true metasurface, Devlin says Metalenz has already replicated the technology in the lab using its own metasurface optics.

“It's really then bringing all of that information together through a single approach," Devlin says. "We would do a metasurface design where now from a single image sensor, you're getting all of the information that is in light: You're getting polarization, you're getting color without filtering, and you're getting this depth channel. It's like the one sensor to rule them all.”

For now, Devlin says the two technologies will be separate products for different markets, but in the long term they could fuse into one Metalenz system. He expects we could see PxE's HoloCoder used in consumer electronics as early as late 2027 or early 2028.

The PxE HoloCoder can detect depth, which can be helpful for autonomous vehicles, without relying on multiple sensors or bulky lidar systems.

Simplifying and shrinking the hardware with metasurface optics was just the first phase for the company—the real goal has always been to unlock that new information channel, which Devlin thinks can be transformational for other categories, like autonomous robots and autonomous vehicles. Instead of relying on large modules with multiple sensors and computationally expensive chips to align all that spatial data in real time, a single-sensor system could do the job in a smaller, cheaper design while using less computing power.

“It is a real problem in the sense that, in the color filter, you lose a lot of light,” says Arka Majumdar, who researches low-energy opto-electronics at the University of Washington. He points out that other industry heavyweights, including Samsung and a startup called Eyeo, have been actively researching their own alternatives to Bayer filters, called “color routers.”

While he agrees that ditching the filter can meaningfully improve smartphone photography in low light, he is skeptical that it can revolutionize categories like robotics and self-driving cars. Unlike phones, vehicles have plenty of space to mount stereo cameras or lidar. The bottleneck isn't low light or image clarity, but the computational power needed to make split-second decisions.

“In fact, arguably, if you get better data, it's actually worse,” he says.

#575. EU's 'Made in Europe' push unnerves global auto suppliers

In shielding Europe's carmakers from Chinese rivals, the EU risks hurting close partners from Turkey and Morocco to Japan and South Korea. Billions in trade and hundreds of thousands of European jobs are at stake.

It is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices. The European Union's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), proposed in March, seeks to upgrade European car factories and only subsidize vehicles produced in Europe.

Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" plan is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains.

After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other key players in the automotive sector, however, will be excluded — including Turkey, which has enjoyed seamless access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.

While the proposals still face major legislative hurdles in Brussels before becoming law, Ayhan Zeytinoglu, chairman of the Economic Development Foundation (IKV), thinks the Franco-German framework could be devastating for Turkey's auto sector.

"73% of Turkey’s total automotive exports go to the EU," Zeytinoglu told DW. "If we encounter a 'Made in Europe' barrier in the EU market, this will cause great damage to our trade with the EU and to our exports."

Excluding Turkey would also harm European automaking rather than strengthen competitiveness against China, he added.

Turkey's auto exporters association OIB calculated that the country's automotive exports to the EU totaled $30.1 billion (€26.8 billion) last year.

The IAA requires that 70% of the total value of a vehicle's components — excluding the battery — should be made in Europe.

However, the initial proposal only applies to battery-electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids and fuel-cell models, which last year made up just 27% of all new EU car registrations.

Tommaso Pardi, director of the international automotive research network GERPISA and a senior researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), notes that the 70% target is remarkably generous.

"If you take an average European-made electric car and take away the battery, you would find that around 83% [of parts] come from Europe," Pardi told DW.

Under the revised German-French plan, some self-charging hybrids and petrol and diesel vehicles could still be sold after 2035 and would also be affected by the "Made in Europe" rules.

These cars contain a much lower proportion of European parts. Most of Turkey's nearly 800,000 vehicle exports to the EU last year would fall under this much larger umbrella.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another key reason for excluding Turkey is that Chinese automakers are expanding their presence there, hoping to gain back-door access to the EU market, but face major roadblocks.

They include SWM Motors, whose factory in the northwestern city of Eskisehir closed within a year because the cars produced didn't meet EU safety standards.

BYD's plans to open a $1 billion plant in Manisa — a large industrial hub near the Aegean coast — have been put on hold.

Morocco, meanwhile, has received Chinese investments worth more than €10 billion ($11 billion) since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to consultancy AlixPartners, much of it in batteries and auto parts.

For France, the North African nation plays a similar role to China for Germany's auto sector — a low-cost production hub that helps French carmakers stay competitive. Budget-friendly French models would likely become more expensive if Morocco were excluded.

Japanese carmakers, which build several of their models in European factories, could also lose out. Cars imported from Japan would not qualify for EU subsidies, while models built in France, Portugal and Eastern Europe would benefit only if enough of their parts come from Europe.

South Korean automakers, meanwhile, could also be hurt. Hyundai and Kia build cars in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, but also ship models from Asia, which would not qualify. Korean battery plants in Poland and Hungary, however, would count as European.

Pardi notes how European car giants are actively lobbying to water down the IAA to protect their high profit margins.

"They want to limit the IAA to retain the biggest scope to still source from abroad, particularly from China," he said.

EU-based automakers warn that higher parts costs would put them at an even bigger disadvantage against Chinese rivals, while European battery supply is unlikely to meet demand anytime soon.

Ankara is also lobbying Brussels to be included in the "Made in Europe" program, while automakers are seeking a compromise that would allow Turkey to join at a later stage.

Pardi said this would be "only for European companies that are based there [Turkey and Morocco] ... while excluding all recent investments involving Chinese capital [in those countries]."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European auto-parts suppliers are, however, on the opposite side of the argument, calling for further strengthening of IAA. They warn that up to 650,000 auto jobs in the region could be lost by 2035 without better protection for their members.

"A lost industrial job is very hard to win back, and the damage reaches well beyond large suppliers," Benjamin Krieger, Secretary General of the European Association of Automotive Suppliers (CLEPA), told DW.

Krieger thinks the IAA helps European industry to level the playing field against unfair competition from China, adding: "We must stop the bleeding."

With broad public support for measures that ensure that EU public funding "benefits value creation in Europe," CLEPA's Krieger thinks allies like Turkey, Morocco, South Korea and Japan may not lose out if they meet the EU's criteria.

"The EU should offer access to the IAA through an opt-in mechanism with objective criteria: regulatory alignment, social and environmental standards, no market distortion, respect for the rule of law and reciprocity, backed by anti-circumvention measures. Partners that meet them are welcome," he said.

#573. Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?

Seagrass protects coasts, shelters thousands of species and stores CO2. But some 30% of this valuable ecosystem has disappeared since the late 19th century. Can we bring it back?

Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, says she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.

"That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped."

Underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.

Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance."

But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.

Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.

"Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he said.

The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.

"We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig said.

Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing new ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.

Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.

"Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.

"The big advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity."

Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.

They then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the new crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.

"We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen said. "It's looking really good."

This article is based on a Global Us video report.

#571. When do Black Friday sales actually start? Official sale times for Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target

If all the emails flooding your inbox weren't enough of an indication, we're closing in on the biggest shopping holiday of the year. Black Friday technically doesn't happen until the dishes from Thanksgiving are scrubbed and put away. But retailers have gotten antsy over the years, kicking off their sales days or weeks in advance. Heck, the whole month of November is basically Black Friday at this point.

If you're hoping to do some discount shopping this holiday season, knowing precisely when to shop each major retailer's official Black Friday sale is key. To help you best strategize this season, we've rounded up the essential dates and times below.

Black Friday always lands on the day after Thanksgiving and the fourth Friday in November. In 2026, that happens to be on Friday, Nov. 27.

As you've probably noticed, however, most major retailers began rolling out early Black Friday deals as soon as the calendar switched to November. Likewise, some will draw things out even longer with Black Friday discounts that last far past the official shopping holiday. Black Friday is no longer a single 24-hour extravaganza; it's a full season.

Cyber Monday, the more online-centric shopping holiday, falls on the Monday after Black Friday. In 2026, that's on Monday, Nov. 30. Most retailers shift into Cyber Monday mode by the Saturday after Black Friday. It's silly, really, but the lines between the two deal-shopping holidays have been blurred beyond recognition.

Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Target tend to have the biggest Black Friday (and Cyber Monday) sales each year, so we've broken down all the nitty gritty details you need to know about each retailer's specific schedule in 2026. Plenty of deals are already live, but if you want to shop the official sales, here's the scoop.

For the second year in a row, Best Buy kicked off its holiday schedule scary early, with its first round of "doorBOOsters" dropping the day before Halloween. The electronics retailer will release new doorbusters on select tech every Friday leading up to the big day.

Best Buy's official Black Friday sale, aka the main event, will run in stores and online from Thursday, Nov. 19 through Saturday, Nov. 28. The calendar then flips to Cyber Monday on Sunday, Nov. 29 and runs through Monday, Nov. 30.

Best Buy's brick-and-mortar stores will be open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time on Black Friday. Want an old-school Black Friday experience? You can camp out at stores if you want to score high-demand items, but Best Buy will employ a ticketing system for customer and employee safety.

All Best Buy stores will be closed on Thanksgiving Day.

Walmart announced plans for three major Black Friday calendar events for 2026. The first is an Early Black Friday Sale, which will take place from Nov. 12 through Nov. 15. The main event, aka the official Black Friday deals event will kick off Monday, Nov. 23 and last through Sunday, Nov. 29. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Deals will be live online only from Nov. 23 through Nov. 26, so in-store shoppers will have to wait until Black Friday proper. Walmart's Cyber Monday sale will take place from Monday, Nov. 30 through Wednesday, Dec. 2 online only.

During both the early and official Black Friday events, select online-only deals will be reserved for Walmart+ members exclusively for the first 24 hours, while supplies last. If you're not a Walmart+ member and want early access to these doorbusters, you can sign up for $12.95/month or $98/year. Trial members are not eligible for early access.

Walmart stores will be open from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. local time on Black Friday. They'll be closed on Thanksgiving Day.

Target launched its first holiday savings event on Nov. 5, with early deals on holiday decor, kitchen appliances, and toys. Its Deal of the Day program also kicked off on Nov. 1 and will run through Dec. 24. Shoppers can score a new featured deal every day of the week until Dec. 24. So far, we've seen 50% off Stanley tumblers and $30 off Apple AirTags.

The official Black Friday shopping event, however, has not properly been announced. If Target follows a similar schedule as last year, we speculate that it'll kick off on Sunday, Nov. 22, and run through Saturday, Nov. 28. The best deals will likely drop exclusively from Nov. 26 through 28 for Black Friday proper. We'll update this with the latest information once it's revealed.

Target Circle 360 members will likely get early access to select deals, as in years past. The savings season will wrap up with Target's Cyber Monday Event from Nov. 29 through Nov. 30 (most likely), featuring online-only deals.

In 2025, Target made the in-store shopping experience worth it by offering the first 100 guests in line a free limited-edition iridescent tote bag, some with gifts inside valued up to $350. We'll be on the lookout for an in-store shopping incentive this year — stay tuned.

Target stores will open at 6 a.m. local time on Black Friday. Closing times vary by location (check your local store). They'll be closed on Thanksgiving, as is company policy.

As in years past, Amazon is hosting a "Black Friday Week" savings event that will kick off on Thursday, Nov. 19 at 3:01 a.m. ET and run through Cyber Monday on Nov. 30. Banners will probably change over from Black Friday to Cyber Monday on Saturday, Nov. 28.

Daily themed deals will drop throughout the event, with "double drops" on Black Friday and Cyber Monday proper at 3 a.m. and 11 a.m. ET.

You don't need to be a Prime member to shop Amazon's Black Friday sale, but it certainly doesn't hurt. There will likely be Prime-exclusive discounts sprinkled here and there throughout the event.

Amazon will also air its fourth annual Black Friday NFL game on Nov. 27 via Prime Video. (The Pittsburgh Steelers host the Denver Broncos, with kickoff slated for 3 p.m. ET) New discounts on toys, electronics, and apparel will be up for grabs during the game. Fans can shop simultaneously as they watch with an enhanced "Shop the Game" experience. There will also be an NBA on Prime doubleheader to follow (Miami Heat vs. New York Knicks and Los Angeles Lakers vs. San Antonio Spurs).

Christina Buff is a Nashville-based freelance writer for who covers shopping with a splash of entertainment. If you’re ever wondering what streaming service you need to watch something (and the cheapest way to sign up for it), she’s your girl.

Christina received a B.S. in Business Communication (concentration in writing) from Stevenson University and began her professional journey writing and editing press releases. Since then, she’s written content for a marketing agency, blogged for celebrities, and covered local news, politics, women’s lifestyle, fashion, beauty, and just about everything in between for various publications.

When she’s not writing, she’s probably enjoying live music, studying human design, or embroidering and upcycling clothes. You can follow her on Instagram at @touchinfinity.

#570. Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany's health scare highlights the need for better support for elite coaches

Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.

Vincent Kompany has just returned home from hospital. The Bayern Munich head coach admitted that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

Bayern Munich's sporting director Max Eberl, who left Gladbach in 2022 due to his own health concerns, told German public broadcaster ARD that the 40-year-old Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation, which if untreated can become meningitis.

"They found out what it is. It is a meningeal irritation that brought on the incident last Friday," said Eberl, referring to when Kompany collapsed during training and required an emergency doctor.

"Honestly, he is doing as well as can be expected. He has been discharged from hospital today, which is the biggest and best news for all of us."

The news has been met by great concern from the German football community. Bayern fans held a banner showing their support, many German media outlets wrote opinion articles softly reminding that coaches are humans too and they too need support. Even the wider coaching community has started to ask questions.

"It’s something you take to heart and think about," Freiburg head coach Julian Schuster said after his team lost to Bayern recently.

"We coaches aren’t always very good at taking care of ourselves in those situations."

Eberl, though, shut down the suggestion that this was related to pressure or stress.

"It's an illness. Any one of us can get it. It has nothing to do with the pressure we face in the Bundesliga," Eberl said.

Nevertheless, with Kompany admitting he hadn't listened to his body and his assistant coach Aaron Danks saying that "getting Vince to rest is a challenge", it is clear that the Belgian had been working very hard of late.

Kompany, whose father became the first Black mayor in Belgium after moving there from the DR Congo, has faced an enormous amount of adversity in his life. At just 14, his parents divorced and he told The Guardian in a 2019 interview: "I need to be fed stuff constantly, otherwise I don’t know how to function. I can't remember a lazy Sunday."

The Belgian's own history, both in his childhood and as former professional player, also plays a role in understanding the challenges coaches face in elite sport.

"I think we (coaches) have a really poor measure of ourselves within this example of like, wasn't listening to my body. I think a lot of coaches are really poor at that,"  coaching mentor Cody Royle, who has worked with teams in the NBA and the Premier League, told DW.

"And so part of my role is to enhance their attunement to that, to ask questions to that effect, to try to perhaps even impart some things that I've learned along the way or heard from others or other coaches that are going through similar things so that you can actually start to put words to what that feeling might have been or where you maybe touched burnout but it didn't quite get there and you're able to rescue something and start to really develop skill within it," he said.

"I think with Vincent's example we also need to account for the fact that this is a young man still finding his way in coaching and so he's still understanding what those triggers are within his body and what they're really telling him Maybe he had physical things that he could read when he was playing. These are more mental triggers, and he's still learning that and that's part of what he needs to do. But there should be people around that help."

It begs the question, in 2026, at a time when awareness around mental and physical health is greater than ever, particularly in elite sport, how is this still possible?

"I suspect that many head coaches aren't able to let go or delegate," Frank Wormuth, an educator for the German Football Association (DFB), told DW.

"They want to control everything because they don't feel secure when the team loses," continued Wormuth, adding that that's why coaches often bring close friends into their staff.

"You'd think professional coaches wouldn't have to worry, since they've earned enough money, but that’s not a good coach's priority—success is far more important."

A former coach, Wormuth admits that he had moments in his career when he had lost sight of how much of a role football was playing in his life.

"I never felt like I was doing too much until my kids pointed out to me—when I was at home—that I wasn't the coach anymore, but should be fulfilling the role of a father," Wormuth said.

"That's when I realized that I was truly operating 24/7 as a coach in my head, even when I was at home."

To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

Royle believes coaches need to learn more about how to manage themselves.

"I kind of throw my hands up a little bit at the fact that we aren't further along," Royle said.

"We're not even trying to educate this in to our young coaches as they come through. The education system probably facilitates this as much as the organizations that are individually responsible."

Clearly, if not well managed, extremely demanding elite-sports environments with high expectations on individuals makes for a dangerous combination. Both Wormuth and Royle advocate for the concept of a second set of eyes.

"Maybe it is that there's a mechanism now for coaches to really investigate," Royle said.

Having someone who sits outside the organization and doesn't belong to the politics to be able to —whether it's on the phone or come in for a visit — just say, 'You need to go home because this isn't going well.'"

"This is a game where Jock Stein literally dropped dead on the sideline, right? There shouldn't need to be any more conversation beyond that... and it was workaholism and stress that caused it," added Royle.

"So I don't know what else it's going to take, but I just don't think the game really cares enough to change anything about it. The show must go on, right?"

Even as it does when Bayern Munich play Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga's most marketed game this weekend, Kompany's absence will serve as a reminder that while much of the focus of modern sport is on the players, there is an equal level of support required for those on the sidelines.
